query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment—specifically, a moderate cold rolling (~8% reduction) followed by a low-temperature annealing step—will modify the uniform fine-lamellar structure of the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA into an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that exhibits improved strength, ductility, and enhanced resistance to creep and corrosion under extreme service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure and suboptimal mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Apply a combined thermo-mechanical processing route consisting of cold rolling (approximately 8% thickness reduction) followed by a controlled, low-temperature annealing treatment to promote microstructural refinement and partial recrystallization.
generation.conditions: Intended for service conditions involving extreme temperature fluctuations (room temperature up to about 700°C), long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep scenarios), and exposure to corrosive environments typical for fastener applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to produce an ultrafine-grained duplex (composite-like) microstructure that inherits a two-hierarchical constrained lamellar architecture. This refined structure can enhance dislocation interactions and grain boundary strengthening while promoting microcrack arrest.
generation.mechanism: Cold work increases dislocation density, while subsequent annealing triggers partial recrystallization that refines the lamellar spacing. The resulting duplex microstructure creates strong phase boundaries and a two-level constraint effect, which helps impede dislocation motion, reduce creep rates, and may improve passivation behavior in corrosive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should exhibit a significant increase in yield and fracture strength (with a target relative improvement, e.g., exceed 10% over the as-cast condition), retain or improve ductility, and demonstrate enhanced resistance to room-temperature creep and corrosion compared to the starting material.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, uniform fine-lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which currently shows a combination of high fracture strength and ductility that is still below industrial requirements for fastener applications in harsh environments.
generation.boundary: Performance improvements are expected primarily in the temperature range from room temperature to about 700°C under mechanical loading and in standard corrosive test solutions. The intervention’s efficacy must be validated under these operating and test boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement values (e.g., percentage increases in strength, creep resistance, and corrosion rate reduction) are uncertain until further systematic testing. The optimal processing parameters (reduction percentage and annealing temperature/time) may require refinement for specific application conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set will remain as the as-cast control, and the other will undergo the proposed cold rolling (~8% reduction) and subsequent low-temperature annealing. Both sets will then be subjected to standardized mechanical (tensile and creep tests up to 700°C) and corrosion tests (using a relevant aggressive solution).
measurements: Yield strength and fracture strength from tensile tests
Creep rate under constant load at room temperature and elevated temperatures
Corrosion rate as measured by standard electrochemical methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements—defined as at least a 10% increase in yield/fracture strength, improved ductility without severe loss, reduced creep rate, and lower corrosion rate compared to the as-cast samples—the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
